ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the prism cross section is triangle ABC, AC is the vertical side, BC is the horizontal side, AB is the oblique side, and C is a right angle. The incident ray is directed horizontally from the left toward the inclined surface AB, with its direction parallel to BC; after entering the prism, the ray propagates obliquely downward to the right, reaches the vertical side AC, and then exits. A horizontal dashed line is drawn at AC, representing the normal of this emergent surface, and an angle θ is marked between the emergent ray and this horizontal normal. The problem gives ∠A = θ = 60°. Reasoning: Since the triangle is right-angled at C, and ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 30°. Therefore the angle between the inclined surface AB and the horizontal side BC is 30°. The angle between the normal of AB and the horizontal incident ray is 60°, so the first angle of incidence i1 = 60°. Let the downward deflection angle of the ray inside the prism relative to the horizontal line be α; then when it reaches the vertical surface AC, the angle of incidence relative to the horizontal normal of AC is α. The first refraction is from air into the prism, and Snell's law is sin60° = n sin(60° − α). The second refraction is from the prism into air, and Snell's law is n sinα = sinθ = sin60°. Combining the two equations gives sin(60° − α) = sinα, so α = 30°. Substituting into n sinα = sin60° gives n = sin60° / sin30° = (√3/2)/(1/2) = √3. The propagation speed of light in the prism v = c/n = c/√3 = (√3/3)c.

As shown in the figure is the cross-section of a right-angled prism. A light ray is incident parallel to the edge $BC$ and, after refraction by the prism, exits from the edge $AC$. It is known that $\angle A=\theta=60^{\circ}$, and the speed of light in a vacuum is $c$.

1. What is the refractive index of the prism material?
2. What is the speed of light propagation in a prism?
ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure is the cross-section of a right-angled prism. A light ray is incident parallel to the edge $BC$ and, after refraction by the prism, exits from the edge $AC$. It is known that $\angle A=\theta=60^{\circ}$, and the speed of light in a vacuum is $c$. 1. What is the refractive index of the prism material? 2. What is the speed of light propagation in a prism?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure, the prism cross-section is triangle ABC, AC is the vertical side, BC is the horizontal side, AB is the hypotenuse, and there is a right angle at C. The incident ray travels horizontally from the left toward the inclined surface AB, with its direction parallel to BC; after the ray enters the prism, it propagates obliquely downward to the right, and exits after reaching the vertical side AC. A horizontal dashed line is drawn at AC, representing the normal to this exit surface, and an angle θ is marked between the exiting ray and this horizontal normal. The problem gives ∠A = θ = 60°.

Reasoning: Since the triangle has a right angle at C, and ∠A = 60°, therefore ∠B = 30°. Therefore the angle between the inclined surface AB and the horizontal side BC is 30°. The angle between the normal to AB and the horizontal incident ray is 60°, so the first angle of incidence i1 = 60°. Let the downward deflection angle of the ray inside the prism relative to the horizontal line be α; then when it reaches the vertical surface AC, its angle of incidence relative to the horizontal normal of AC is α. For the first refraction from air into the prism, Snell's law is sin60° = n sin(60° − α). For the second refraction from the prism into air, Snell's law is n sinα = sinθ = sin60°. Combining the two equations gives sin(60° − α) = sinα, so α = 30°. Substituting into n sinα = sin60°, gives n = sin60° / sin30° = (√3/2)/(1/2) = √3. The propagation speed of light in the prism is v = c/n = c/√3 = (√3/3)c.
